subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
passage:
Counsellor's note. Tejas came with his father, Hrithik, to discuss whether Tejas should take a local job or apply for a master's programme in another city. Hrithik favoured the job: "Experience first, degrees later."

Tejas did not roll his eyes or go silent. He asked, "What did you see happen to people who studied first?" Hrithik described a colleague whose degree led nowhere. Tejas listened and said, "That's a real risk. I see it differently: I think the programme fits my field. I'll apply, and if I don't get funding I'll take the job. I'll be the one to answer for the decision."

Hrithik crossed his arms but nodded. On the way out he said, "Send me the list of programmes."

I suggested they meet again after the results, and that Tejas keep his father informed at each step rather than hiding anything.

qa.a: The job. He said "Experience first, degrees later."

qa.q: What does Tejas's question about people who studied first suggest about his attitude?
qa.a: That he respects his father's experience and wants to understand the reasons rather than dismiss them.

qa.q: What could Tejas do next to keep the disagreement respectful?
qa.a: Apply as planned, keep his father informed at each step, and be ready to own the outcome, as the counsellor suggests.

qa.q: How might Hrithik have felt during the conversation?
qa.a: Concerned for his son's security. Crossing his arms and then nodding suggest reluctant acceptance, and asking for the list shows he is willing to stay involved.

grounding: Tejas disagrees with his father yet respects his experience, seeks his reasons, differs politely and owns the decision, seen by a counsellor.

subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
passage:
The offer from the Bengaluru firm had to be accepted by 6 p.m., and it was already 4:30 when Madhuri finally got her mother on a crackling line from Nani's village.
"Beta, stay in Nagpur. Your father's cousin can get you into the bank here."
Madhuri's first instinct was to say, "You don't understand my field," and hang up. Her sister Simran, beside her, raised an eyebrow.
"Mummy, can I ask why you want me here? Really why."
The line crackled. "When I was twenty-two I went to Pune alone and was so lonely I cried every night. I don't want that for you."
Madhuri swallowed. "Thank you for telling me. I didn't know that. I still think Bengaluru is right for me. I'll find a PG with girls from my team, call you every night, and if I'm miserable after six months, I'll tell you honestly."
Silence, then: "You're an adult. Just call."
At 5:48 she clicked accept, Simran cheering beside her.

qa.q: By what time did the offer have to be accepted?
Why did Madhuri swallow after hearing her mother's story?
qa.a: She felt moved and a little ashamed of her dismissive first instinct, understanding that her mother's fear came from lonely years in Pune.
She asked for her mother's real reason, thanked her, stated her own decision, and offered concrete comfort: a PG with teammates, nightly calls and an honest check at six months.

qa.q: How does Madhuri's mother see the move?
qa.a: Through her own lonely time in Pune; she still worries, but accepts that Madhuri is an adult.

grounding: Shows disagreeing with a parent while respecting their experience: asking their reasons, differing politely and owning the decision.

subtopic: Parents pressure on career or marriage
passage:
Kavitha had the flat's rental agreement in her bag when she sat down with her parents in their Chennai living room. Ira, her college friend, had already paid her half of the deposit.
"Why do you need a separate flat when home is fifteen kilometres away?" her father asked.
Kavitha had rehearsed a speech about independence. She set it aside. "Appa, what worries you about it most?"
He took off his glasses. "People will talk. And if you fall sick at night, who will be there?"
"Ira will. And I'll come home every Sunday. The commute from here is two hours a day; from the flat it's twenty minutes." She paused. "I know you've seen more of the world than me. I'm still choosing this. If it goes badly, that's on me, and I'll say so."
Amma looked at Appa for a long moment. "She's thought about it," she said.
Appa sighed. "Sundays. And you'll call if you're unwell."
"Promise."

qa.q: How far is home from the flat?
Why did Kavitha set aside her rehearsed speech?
qa.a: She felt calmer and wanted to understand Appa's worry rather than argue, which showed her respect for him.

qa.q: What made Kavitha's decision an adult one?
qa.a: She heard Appa's reasons, answered them concretely, and said she would own the outcome if it went badly.

qa.q: How does Amma see Kavitha's plan?
qa.a: As thought through; she backs Kavitha by saying so to Appa.

grounding: Illustrates respectful disagreement with parents: seeking their reasons, differing politely and deciding as an adult who owns the outcome.
